title: Home & everyday objects
goal: Name rooms and household objects, say where things are, and say what there is (and isn't) in a place.
intro:
A traditional Kerala house has an ഉമ്മറം (*ummaṟam*, front veranda) where guests are received, and the kitchen is often at the back. Modern flats and houses look much like anywhere else — but you will still take your shoes off at the door.

The grammar here is **location**: the ending **-ഇൽ** (-il, 'in/at/on') and positional words such as മുകളിൽ 'on top of', അടിയിൽ 'under', അടുത്ത് 'near'. Malayalam uses **postpositions** — they come *after* the noun.

vocab.note: Toilet: ടോയ്‌ലറ്റ് / ബാത്ത്‌റൂം are very common.

phrases.en: How many rooms are there in this house?
Could you switch on the fan?

grammar.title: The locative -ഇൽ and positional postpositions
grammar.body:
'In / at / on' is the ending **-ഇൽ** (-il). Before it:
• vowels add a glide: മുറി → മുറി**യിൽ**, മേശ → മേശ**യിൽ**
• -ം becomes -ത്ത-: പുസ്തകം → പുസ്തക**ത്തിൽ**
• short words in -ട് / -റ് double the consonant: വീട് → വീ**ട്ടിൽ**, ആറ് → ആ**റ്റിൽ** 'in the river'
• chillu letters revert to the full letter: കട്ടിൽ → കട്ടി**ലിൽ**, വാതിൽ → വാതി**ലിൽ**

More precise positions use a **postposition** after the noun, usually in the possessive (-ഉടെ / -ന്റെ): മേശ**യുടെ മുകളിൽ** 'on top of the table', കട്ടി**ലിന്റെ അടിയിൽ** 'under the bed', വീ**ടിന്റെ മുന്നിൽ** 'in front of the house'. A handy compound: മേശപ്പുറത്ത് 'on the table (surface)'.

examples.en: The book is in the cupboard.
The cat is under the bed.
The car is in front of the house.

grammar.title: 'There is' (ഉണ്ട്) vs 'is' (ആണ്)
grammar.body:
Malayalam has two 'be' words:

• **ഉണ്ട്** *uṇḍŭ* = **exists / there is / is (located)**. Negative **ഇല്ല**. Used for 'there is a fan in the room', 'the key is (to be found) on the table', and for possession (unit 3).
• **ആണ്** *āṇŭ* = **is (identity / description)**. Negative **അല്ല**. Used for 'this is my room', and also for *stating* a location as a fact: താക്കോൽ മേശപ്പുറത്താണ് 'the key is on the table (that's where it is)'.

So: ഇല്ല ↔ ഉണ്ട്, അല്ല ↔ ആണ്. Mixing them up (*ഫാൻ അല്ല* for 'there's no fan') is a classic learner mistake. Note also ആരും + ഇല്ല 'nobody', ഒന്നും + ഇല്ല 'nothing'.

examples.en: There is a fan in the room.
There's no TV in the room.

dialogue.title: Renting a house
dialogue.setting: Mr Varghese, the owner, shows a house to David, who wants to rent it.

lines.speaker: Varghese
lines.en: Come inside. This is the hall.

lines.speaker: David
lines.native: നല്ല വലിയ മുറി. ഈ വീട്ടിൽ എത്ര മുറികൾ ഉണ്ട്?
lines.roman: nalla valiya muṟi. ī vīṭṭil etra muṟikaḷ uṇḍŭ?
lines.en: Nice big room. How many rooms are there in this house?

lines.speaker: Varghese
lines.native: രണ്ട് കിടപ്പുമുറികൾ ഉണ്ട്. ഒന്ന് മുകളിൽ, ഒന്ന് താഴെ.
lines.roman: raṇḍŭ kiṭappumuṟikaḷ uṇḍŭ. onnŭ mukaḷil, onnŭ tāḻe.
lines.en: There are two bedrooms. One upstairs, one downstairs.

lines.speaker: Varghese
lines.en: Behind the hall. The bathroom is next to the kitchen.

lines.speaker: David
lines.en: Are there fans in the rooms?

lines.speaker: David
lines.en: No problem. Is there a bed and a wardrobe?

lines.speaker: Varghese
lines.native: ഉണ്ട്, രണ്ട് മുറിയിലും ഉണ്ട്. ഇതാ താക്കോൽ.
lines.roman: uṇḍŭ, raṇḍŭ muṟiyilum uṇḍŭ. itā tākkōl.
lines.en: Yes, in both rooms. Here's the key.

culture: Shoes are left outside the door, and the kitchen and prayer room are especially 'clean' spaces. Guests are seated on the ഉമ്മറം or in the front hall and offered tea or water almost immediately. Note that switching things on/off uses English: ഓൺ ചെയ്യുക, ഓഫ് ചെയ്യുക — or the native ഇടുക 'put (on)' and കെടുത്തുക 'put out'.
